title: What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
detail:
What the Big Banks' Third-Quarter Reports Say About Credit Card Borrowers
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 8:35 AM CDT 5 min read
MA
BAC
JPM
C
COF

Trading disclosure

Credit cards are a huge benefit and a huge risk because they make it easy to spend. And since you don't have to pay the bill for 30 days or so, the hit can sometimes take consumers by surprise. This is why you can get an important read on consumers by looking at the credit card businesses of large banks like Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Citigroup (NYSE: C), and Capital One (NYSE: COF). The read after the third quarter: the consumer is looking good. Here's the proof.

Banks take on the credit risk

While credit cards usually carry the logos of companies like Visa (NYSE: V) or Mastercard (NYSE: MA), those companies are just payment processors. They charge small fees for facilitating financial transactions; the banks that issue the credit cards bear the financial risk. If a customer doesn't pay their credit card bill, banks like Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, and Capital One have to eat the cost.

Image source: Getty Images.

That said, issuing credit cards can be a very profitable business. So there's a balance that has to be struck between risk and reward. And when it comes to the risk side, banks tell you each quarter what's going on. They do this by reporting their 30-day and 90-day delinquency ratios and charge-off ratios. You just have to dig into the financial releases to find the data.

Everything is OK for now

Citigroup's credit card operations had a 30-day delinquency ratio of 1.16% in its own branded card portfolio in the third quarter. In cards it issues for other companies, often called private-label cards, that ratio was 1.96%. Private-label cards tend to be issued to riskier customers. Still, neither figure is particularly bad, and both are lower than they were a year ago. That same story holds for the 90-day delinquency ratios, which came in at 1.21% for Citigroup's cards and 1.92% for private-label cards.

JPMorgan Chase is the same exact story. The fairly strong 1.97% 30-day delinquency rate was down from a year ago. And the even stronger 90-day delinquency rate of 0.96% was also down from a year ago.

Bank of America's story is no different. Its 30-day delinquency rate stood at 2.32% in the third quarter of 2026, down from the same quarter in 2025. Its 90-day delinquency rate was 1.13%, also down year over year. That said, the company also reports net charge-offs, which came in at 3.22%. Like the delinquency rates, the financial giant's charge-offs were lower than they were a year ago.

Capital One tends to take on lower-credit-quality customers. That's probably why its 3.72% 30-day delinquency rate is higher than the other banks here. However, like the other banks, Capital One's 30-day delinquency rate was lower in the third quarter than it was a year ago. That said, it did tick up slightly from the second quarter's 3.37%. It wasn't the only bank to see a sequential increase from the second quarter, but the jump was easily the biggest here. Still, charge-offs fell sequentially and year-over-year to 4.01%, so it doesn't look like the bank's credit risks are getting out of hand.

It looks like consumers are holding up well

The news is filled with stories about the financial strains that consumers are facing. High inflation may be a pain, as costs increase, but increasingly budget-conscious consumers don't appear to have overextended themselves. At least, that's what the credit card data from some of the world's largest financial companies and credit card issuers suggests.

title: Tech Bonds Are 'Diamonds in the Rough': Bank of America's Hartnett Says
detail:
Tech Bonds Are 'Diamonds in the Rough': Bank of America's Hartnett Says
The Bank of America logo and name are displayed on the exterior of a building, indicating a branch location. (Credit: Image via Shutterstock)

Bank of America's top strategist has found value in an unloved corner of the AI trade: the bonds of the companies paying for it.

"Buy tech bond 'diamonds-in-rough' as AI hyperscalers up equity issuance, cut buybacks," Michael Hartnett, chief investment strategist at Bank of America, said in his latest Flow Show note.

The call comes after a punishing year for tech credit.

Why Hartnett Calls Tech Bonds 'Diamonds in the Rough'

According to Hartnett, U.S. technology bonds have lost about 9% so far in 2026.

That leaves their total return relative to the broad investment-grade bond index at the lowest level in 30 years. In other words, tech debt has rarely looked this cheap compared with the rest of the high-grade market.

The main reason is supply. AI hyperscalers have sold $182 billion of bonds this year, up from just $17 billion in 2024, as they borrow to build data centers.

Investors have demanded higher yields to absorb that wave. As a result, long-dated bonds of the Magnificent Seven and other AI leaders now yield between 6% and 8%, a level Hartnett considers attractive.

Further down the credit ladder, the 2031 high-yield bond of CoreWeave Inc. yields 14.26%.

Why Bondholders Are Gaining the Upper Hand

The second part of Hartnett's argument concerns how the hyperscalers are now raising money.

Meta's recent share sale, he said, signals a new respect for credit investors. Selling stock rather than adding more debt strengthens the balance sheet that bondholders rely on.

Hartnett also believes the long stretch in which AI bonds lagged AI stocks is coming to an end.

Hyperscalers have raised $89 billion through equity issuance in 2026. At the same time, their share buybacks are running at an annualized pace of just $14 billion, down from $105 billion in 2024.

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your 'Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

For Hartnett, that means the era of big stock buybacks is over. Cash that used to flow back to shareholders is now being kept inside the companies, which in turn favors those who own the debt.

The pressure comes from spending. Bank of America estimates AI capital expenditure will climb from $240 billion in 2024 to $1.2 trillion in 2027. Over the same period, free cash flow is seen swinging from $240 billion to negative $180 billion.

For this reason, Hartnett said, bond markets are now policing the AI boom.

S&P Global Data Show Credit Markets Are Still Nervous

The bond market has not given the all-clear yet.

Five-year credit default swaps, which show the annual cost of insuring a company's debt against default, have widened sharply across Big Tech since early September, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence data as of Friday.

Oracle's spread rose to 276 basis points from 210 on Sept. 1. Nvidia's climbed to 129 from 84, while Meta's increased to 118 from 94.

Alphabet Inc. moved to 85 from 61, and Amazon to 90 from 67. Microsoft remained the safest name, at 55 from 47.

However, there are early signs of stabilization. Oracle's spread has eased from a peak of 325 basis points on Oct. 20.

S&P Global has flagged a deeper shift. In an Oct. 13 update, it said spreads on AI-exposed tech companies have widened even as the broader investment-grade market has held up.

Investors, S&P Global said, increasingly treat AI exposure as a distinct credit risk. In addition, rising correlations among hyperscalers, chipmakers and other AI issuers mean tech credit is starting to trade as a single theme, eroding the diversification benefits of holding several names.

Supply will not fade soon. S&P Global said hyperscaler-related bond issuance reached about $240 billion in the first three quarters, on pace for its $250 billion to $300 billion full-year estimate.

See Also: Skip the Regrets: The Essential Retirement Tips Experts Wish Everyone Knew Earlier.

The Levels Hartnett Is Watching

Hartnett expects risk-off conditions to persist until the global rate-hiking cycle ends. Central banks have delivered 42 hikes over the past six months.

He sees a release valve in the first half of 2027: geopolitical peace, a collapse in oil prices and the end of rate hikes.

Before any year-end rally, Hartnett said two levels must hold: $70 on the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF and $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

On Friday, MAGS slipped 2.2% to $69.70, just below that line. SMH remains about 8% above its threshold.

Treasury yields offer little relief. The 10-year yield stood at 4.93% and the 30-year at 5.29%. The iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF is down 5.5% this year.

Hartnett's case rests on a simple shift. Shareholders have funded the AI race so far. Now bondholders are being paid more to finance the next leg, even as default-protection costs show that credit markets remain wary.

Building Wealth Across More Than Just the Market

Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That's why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn't tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry.

This allows everyday investors to diversify into real estate, collect rental income, and build long-term wealth without needing to manage properties directly.

As artificial intelligence drives a surge in electricity demand, reliable power generation is becoming a critical part of the technology ecosystem. American PowerGen is developing natural gas-fired power plants in Texas, a fast-growing market fueled by AI data centers, manufacturing expansion, and population growth. By advancing projects through permitting, fuel supply, and grid interconnection, the company is positioning itself to help meet rising energy needs while offering investors exposure to the infrastructure supporting the next wave of AI and industrial growth.

Key Takeaways

Bank of America cut its DoorDash price target to $257 from $275 on Oct. 30 but kept its Buy rating. That target is 44% above a stock that's down 33% in a year.

In the third quarter, DoorDash reported record revenue and profit. It also agreed to buy Instacart for about $17 billion, at least 75% of it in cash.

DoorDash trades at 25x forward earnings, its lowest in five years, and Bank of America's target implies 35x, below the stock's three-year average.

Bank of America's call looks right on the numbers. The risks are the debt and new shares from the Instacart deal and how long it will take to close.

DoorDash (DASH:NASDAQ) just reported record revenue and profit, and agreed to buy Instacart (CART:NASDAQ) for about $17 billion. Its stock is still down 33% from a year ago, at $179 as of Thursday's close.

On Oct. 30, Bank of America analyst Justin Post cut his price target to $257 from $275 and kept his Buy rating. That's 44% upside.

A year of bigger bills

The trouble started in November 2025, when management said it would spend several hundred million dollars more in 2026 on new projects.

That bill showed up in the second quarter of 2026, when diluted EPS fell to $0.46 from $0.65.

Then, on Oct. 29, came a much bigger bill: Instacart at $65 a share, at least 75% in cash.

Bank of America is still a buyer

Post's $257 target matches the Street's average to the dollar, and the quarter backs him up. Third-quarter revenue rose 34% to $4.6 billion, net income jumped 91% to $466 million, and adjusted EBITDA climbed 41% to $1.06 billion, in the top half of management's guidance.

Does $257 add up?

The Street's average target has fallen from $303 a year ago to $257:

DoorDash (DASH): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

Targets run from $172 to $350, and 43 analysts cover the stock.

Analysts cut their 2026 and 2027 normalized EPS estimates over the past year, but they've raised both by 5% to 6% since June 30. They now expect normalized EPS to climb from $5.10 in 2025 to $8.25 in 2027 and $10.16 in 2028:

DoorDash (DASH): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

The quarter's beat should help the 2026 and 2027 estimates hold up. The 2028 estimate is harder to call, since DoorDash plans to reinvest more than all of the Instacart synergies in the first year after closing.

At [$179], DoorDash trades at 25x forward earnings, its lowest in five years. Post's $257 works out to 35x expected earnings over the next twelve months. That's above the stock's one-year average of 33x and below its three-year average of 39x.

Bank of America: Managing Mostly Flat Quarterly Revenue

Bank of America Corp. (NYSE:BAC) primarily generates revenue by providing traditional consumer checking accounts, customized wealth management strategies, and global corporate lending.

While facing multiple securities fraud class action lawsuits and addressing a $1.2 billion penalty from the U.S. Treasury regarding anti-money laundering regulations, it acquired the cybersecurity firm MDSec Consulting Limited and introduced new generative AI capabilities alongside cross-border real-time payment solutions.

JPMorgan Chase: Delivering Consistent Upward Revenue Growth

JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) primarily earns revenue by offering retail banking accounts, commercial investment vehicles, and dedicated institutional asset management.

It entered a $20 billion strategic asset management partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority and invested in sustainable forestry in Paraguay, while expanding its consumer offerings by removing foreign transaction fees from specific credit cards and launching a phased rollout for a new data security center.

All three main equity indexes gapped down at Friday's open, as the rotation out of technology and artificial intelligence infrastructure accelerated to a frightful pace on All Hallows Eve. Investors, traders and speculators are seeking safety in energy, consumer staples and healthcare stocks, as well as Treasury bonds, amid rising concern about capex plans and return on AI.

By the closing bell, the Nasdaq Composite had fallen 2.9% to 25,437, the tech-heavy index's steepest single-day decline since March 2025, turning what had been a modest weekly gain into a 2% weekly loss.

The broad-based S&P 500 was off 1.8% at 7,580, resulting in a 0.6% decline for the week. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.1% today to 51,770. Papa Dow dipped 0.9% this week.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," LPL Financial Chief Cross-Asset Strategist Adam Turnquist observes. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."

Alphabet (GOOGL, -1.4%) reported its weakest ad revenue growth in five quarters, while e-commerce sales for Amazon (AMZN, -1.4%) slowed to a three-year low. But Microsoft (MSFT, -1.6%) reported a nice pop for cloud revenue, including expectations-beating Azure sales.

Track all markets on TradingView

Still, according to Turnquist, the Magnificent 7 stocks are showing signs of weakness from a technical perspective.

Indeed, the Magnificent Seven Index has broken below support near its May highs and is approaching another key level. Relative strength "is also at a critical inflection point," with more deterioration from here suggesting leadership "is rotating away from mega-cap stocks."

The wider technology complex was also destabilized on Friday by a reported $6.3 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance engineered by agents of North Korea's government.

Intel is way outside

Intel (INTC, -28.6%) was the worst S&P 500 stock on Friday after management reported mixed results and offered weak guidance, amid a more-rapid-than-anticipated deceleration for its core PC market.

The chipmaker expects to report earnings of 25 cents per share for the fourth quarter on revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion. Wall Street forecast EPS of 45 cents on revenue of $17.3 billion.

Track all markets on TradingView

Other semiconductor stocks got dragged down, too, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD, -10.9%), which is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Tuesday.

Nvidia (NVDA, -4.2%) was the worst Dow Jones stock. Fellow Mag 7ers Meta Platforms (META, -1.5%) and Tesla (TSLA, -0.9%) looked better by comparison.

Track all markets on TradingView

Apple (AAPL, -1.2%) will be the sixth Magnificent 7 stock to report this season when it reveals fiscal fourth-quarter results after Monday's closing bell.

As Turnquist explains, AAPL outperformed this month because the iPhone maker is "more asset-light compared to peers" and is still generating strong positive free cash flow.

Crude oil up, bond yields down

The front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures contract rose 2.4% to $104.45 per barrel, and Brent futures added 1.5% to $112.44, reflecting expectations the war in the Middle East will intensify after midterm elections in the U.S.

The 2-year Treasury yield (-6.4 basis points, 4.592%), as well as the 10-year (-5.8 bps, 4.931%) and the 30-year (-1.9 bps, 5.31%), declined as investors bid up bond prices in their search for safety.

Meanwhile, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) will share its October update on the employment situation before the opening bell next Friday. Markets expect the data to reflect continuing stability.

Indeed, even after a cooler-than-expected September jobs report, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remains focused on the inflation problem.

That includes Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who dissented from the decision to hold interest rates steady at the October Fed meeting and promises to generate economic calendar sparks next Thursday.

Note that the Treasury Department announced an I-bond rate of 5.51%, which is fixed for the six months through April 30, 2027, and looks even more attractive after today's price action.

What is it about Berkshire Hathaway?

Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B, +0.3%), because of what's inside Warren Buffett's and Greg Abel's portfolio, is a lot like an equity index fund. It's actually the biggest financial stock in the S&P 500.

But Berkshire's holdings include American Express (AXP, -1.4%) and Bank of America (BAC, -2.2%), as well as Apple, which remains the biggest holding, and Alphabet, which will go down as Buffett's last major equity buy.

Track all markets on TradingView

It also includes consumer staples such as Coca-Cola (KO, +1.4%), energy stocks such as Chevron (CVX, +1.7%) and industrials such as Delta Air Lines (DAL, -1.8%).

Today, the blue chip stock traded like a safe haven. Next Saturday, Abel's team will report quarterly earnings for the first time since Buffett's retirement as chairman of the board in September.

Reddit's (RDDT) Q3 user miss was driven by weaker search-referral traffic, which declined further in October, with current trends pointing to a low-double-digit decline in daily active users in Q4, BofA Securities said Friday in a note.

Reddit's Q3 revenue was $895 million, exceeding Street estimates. Q3 daily active users were 130.3 million, below the Street consensus, driven by a decline in Google search referral traffic, according to the note.

The company is shifting marketing spend toward app installs and plans to test a logged-in-only experience internationally in Q4, BofA noted. The firm expects the transition to a logged-in user experience to take multiple quarters and weigh on headline traffic trends, the note added.

However, the change could result in a higher quality user base, improve monetization and eliminate the Google traffic overhang, the brokerage said. BofA expects sentiment to remain subdued for a few quarters until Reddit demonstrates positive growth momentum for US logged-in users.

BofA kept a neutral rating on Reddit and lowered its price target to $135 from $190.

Shares of Reddit were down 26% in Friday trading.

Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL, XETRA:APC) is expected to deliver a modest earnings beat for its September quarter, but a staggered iPhone launch, rising component costs and weaker services growth could weigh on its December results, according to Bank of America (BofA).

The brokerage expects September-quarter revenue of $113 billion and earnings per share of $1.97, compared with Wall Street estimates of $114 billion and $1.99, respectively, ahead of results due after the market closes on November 2.

The bank said the staggered launch of new iPhone models would affect quarterly sales patterns, with the Pro, Pro Max and Duo models released in September, while the base model and Air are scheduled for March.

The brokerage lowered its financial 2027 iPhone shipment forecast by 9 million units to 247 million, compared with the Street estimate of 260 million, reflecting a more cautious view of demand.

It expects component cost inflation, particularly for memory, to put pressure on gross margins over the coming quarters, although higher prices, product mix and cost-saving measures should offset part of the impact.

BofA estimates that memory costs could reduce iPhone gross margins by 900 basis points before pricing, mix and cost actions narrow the impact to 500 basis points, with the overall effect on company gross margin estimated at 250 basis points.

The brokerage forecasts total gross margin of 43.6% to 44.6% in the March quarter, below the 47.7% consensus estimate, and said the pressure should prove temporary, with margins recovering towards the end of financial 2027 and into financial 2028.

Services revenue is another concern, with BofA expecting growth of 10% in the September quarter, while App Store revenue growth slowed to 1.8% from 3.8% in the previous quarter.

The brokerage reiterated its 'buy' rating and $370 price target, but cautioned that near-term results could face headwinds relative to market expectations.

Starbucks Corp (NASDAQ:SBUX, XETRA:SRB) is showing signs of a sustained business recovery, with stronger US sales, improving profitability and cost savings supporting its latest earnings beat, while Jefferies and Bank of America (BofA) see scope for further progress in financial 2027.

The coffee chain reported US same-store sales growth of 7.7% in the fourth quarter, ahead of the 7% analyst consensus, driven by a 2.4% increase in customer traffic and a 5.2% rise in average spending.

Adjusted earnings per share were $0.80, beating the 72-cent consensus estimate, while operating margin increased to 14%, against expectations of 12.7%, as lower store operating expenses and general and administrative costs supported profitability.

International same-store sales grew 0.9%, below the 3.3% consensus, as stronger performance in the UK was offset by weaker results in Japan.

Jefferies said product innovation, rewards, delivery and improvements to stores were contributing to the recovery, with more than 1,700 store upgrades completed by the end of financial 2026 and another 2,000 planned for financial 2027.

Starbucks forecast North American same-store sales growth of 4% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.15 to $3.25 for financial 2027, broadly in line with the $3.16 analyst consensus at the midpoint.

The company expects operating margin to reach 13.5% to 14%, compared with 11.9% in financial 2026, as cost savings and operational improvements support profitability.

BofA said management had set conservative targets for sales growth and earnings, leaving room for further upgrades as stronger same-store sales and cost reductions flow through to profits.

Jefferies took a more cautious view, forecasting North American same-store sales growth of 3.3% and an operating margin of 13.2% in financial 2027, below management's outlook.

The broker reiterated its 'hold' rating and $101 price target, arguing that investor optimism was already reflected in the valuation and questions remained over the sustainability of the recovery.

BofA raised its price target to $141 from $136, maintaining its positive outlook on the recovery, and said Starbucks could deliver further earnings upgrades as sales growth and cost savings exceed management's conservative forecasts.

Both Bank of America and Roth Capital downgraded Intel to 'Neutral' from 'Buy'.

Bank of America also lowered its estimate of the company's 2030 earnings power.

Citi called Intel's quarterly performance a 'strong beat' but said its December-quarter outlook was 'weak.'

Intel (INTC) shares were on track to wipe out a quarter of their market capitalization and see their worst day in over two years in pre-market trade on Friday after a slew of price target cuts and downgrades from Wall Street following the tech giant's third-quarter earnings.

Analysts broadly agree that Intel's near-term outlook is shaky, with weaker PC demand, manufacturing constraints, and delayed supply improvements weighing on expectations, according to TheFly.

INTC stock fell as much as 25% in pre-market trade, on track to see its biggest single-day dip since July 2024. If the stock falls more than 26%, it would mark its biggest dip since April 1979, when it fell over 33%.

INTC stock daily gains over the past years on October 30 as of 7:30 a.m. ET | Source: Koyfin

If the losses hold through the regular session, the stock would also hit a six-month low. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Intel remained in 'bullish' territory over the past day.

INTC stock retail sentiment on October 30 as of 7:30 a.m. ET | Source: Stocktwits
INTC Stock Gets Downgraded

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to 'Neutral' from 'Buy' and lowered the price target to $100 from $145. He said the company's turnaround had been pushed out by PC and supply headwinds, while a "surprisingly sharp drop" in PC shipments offset strength in data center demand.

Arya also pointed to a lack of progress in attracting outside foundry customers, saying Intel "has not communicated enough traction with external foundry customers." The firm lowered its estimate of Intel's 2030 earnings power to $5 to $6 per share from $6 to $7.

Roth Capital analyst Suji Desilva also downgraded Intel to 'Neutral' from 'Buy' and lowered his price target to $70 from $120. While "encouraged" by continued data center growth and the expansion of Intel's custom data center business, Desilva said manufacturing constraints could limit further upside.

Intel Had A 'Strong Beat' But 'Weak' Outlook

While Citi stated that Intel's third-quarter performance was a "strong beat," it also noted that the company's December-quarter outlook was "weak," citing the impact of a manufacturing accident that shut down Fab 28 in Israel and softer PC demand. The firm lowered its price target to $100 from $130 while maintaining a 'Buy' rating.

Caterpillar's (CAT) strong earnings power remains intact, with potential to grow earnings per share amid the company's conservative guidance and macro uncertainty, BofA Securities said in a Friday note.

The company reported Q3 adjusted profit of $7.20 per share, up from $4.95 a year earlier, as sales and revenue rose to $20.68 billion from $17.64 billion. Caterpillar shares fell after the results and BofA attributed this to a narrow earnings beat.

BofA also noted that Caterpillar did not raise its outlook, even with a record $78 billion backlog, limiting EPS revisions.

Caterpillar's backlog and EPS outlook entail minimal capital requirements, yet the company trades at a free cash flow yield of 5%, the brokerage said. The company still has the potential to generate 15% of its market cap in free cash flow in the coming years, BofA added.

BofA has a buy rating on Caterpillar, with a lower price target of $746 from $850 previously.
